question: What drives the flat panel displays on this airplane?

options.text: The flight control computers
The air data computers directly
Display electronic units that process data from the airplane systems
The flight management computer

explanation: The units gather, validate and format the data, which is why a display failure and a data failure are different problems.

question: What happens if one display electronic unit fails?

options.text: The remaining unit can drive all the displays
The displays continue but without engine indications
The displays revert to the standby instruments
Half the displays are lost

explanation: Either unit is capable of supporting the whole flight deck, so a single failure does not remove any display.

question: What is shown on the primary flight display?

options.text: Navigation aid bearings and distances only
Engine parameters and system status
Attitude, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, heading and mode annunciations
Route information and weather radar

explanation: Everything needed to control the flight path is gathered into one display so the scan stays in one place.

question: What is shown on the navigation display?

options.text: Attitude and airspeed as a backup to the primary display
The lateral situation, including route, navigation aids and weather
Engine secondary indications
Hydraulic and electrical system status

explanation: It answers where the airplane is and what is around it, while the primary display answers what it is doing.

question: What is the purpose of the display source and transfer switching?

options.text: It switches the displays between day and night brightness
It allows a failed display or source to be replaced by the remaining one
It transfers control of the displays to the flight management computer
It selects between metric and imperial units

explanation: Reconfiguration is what preserves the information when a display unit or a data source is lost.

question: Which speeds are normally displayed on the airspeed tape during takeoff?

options.text: The flap placard speeds only
The minimum and maximum manoeuvre speeds only
The takeoff reference speeds such as V1, VR and V2
The selected mode control panel speed only

explanation: Placing the decision speeds on the tape removes the need to read them from a card during the acceleration.

question: What does the amber bar at the lower end of the airspeed tape indicate?

options.text: The flap placard speed
The minimum speed for autopilot engagement
The minimum manoeuvre speed for the current configuration
The stick shaker activation speed

explanation: It marks where manoeuvre margin begins to disappear, which is well above the speed where the stall warning operates.

question: What does the red and black barber pole at the bottom of the airspeed tape represent?

options.text: The reference landing speed
The speed at which the stick shaker operates
The minimum speed for flap extension
The minimum manoeuvre speed

explanation: It is the last speed reference before the stall warning activates, and the space above it is the margin remaining.

question: What does the barber pole at the top of the airspeed tape represent?

options.text: The landing gear operating limit speed
The turbulence penetration speed
The maximum operating speed or Mach number
The flap placard speed for the current setting

explanation: The pole moves with altitude because the limit changes from an airspeed limit to a Mach limit as the airplane climbs.

question: What does the airspeed trend vector show?

options.text: The speed the airplane will reach if the current rate of change continues
The difference between indicated and true airspeed
The speed required for the next flap setting
The speed selected on the mode control panel

explanation: It turns a rate of change into a predicted value, which is what makes an early correction possible.

question: What is the purpose of the pitch limit indication on the attitude display?

options.text: It shows the pitch commanded by the flight director
It shows the maximum pitch for passenger comfort
It shows the pitch limit for tail clearance on rotation
It shows the pitch attitude at which the stall warning would occur

explanation: During a manoeuvre near the limit it is more useful to see the margin in attitude than to interpret the speed tape alone.

question: When does radio altitude normally appear on the primary flight display?

options.text: Only when the landing gear is extended
Below a preset height above the terrain
Whenever the flaps are extended
Only during an ILS approach

explanation: The information becomes relevant only close to the ground. Verify the display threshold against your operator FCOM.

question: What can the minimums reference be set to?

options.text: A barometric altitude only
Either a barometric altitude or a radio height
A flight level only
A radio height only

explanation: The choice reflects the type of approach, since a precision approach with a radio reference is a different case from a barometric minimum.

question: Why is a radio height minimum unsuitable for most non precision approaches?

options.text: Because the terrain profile before the runway makes the radio height unreliable as a reference
Because the radio altimeter is inaccurate above 500 ft
Because the radio altimeter cannot be displayed with a barometric altitude
Because the radio altimeter is only powered with the gear down

explanation: The radio altimeter measures height above whatever is below, which may bear no relation to the height above the runway.

question: Which navigation display mode presents the route against a moving map background?

options.text: APP
PLAN
MAP
VOR

explanation: It shows the airplane in relation to its planned track, which is how the lateral situation is normally monitored.

question: Which navigation display mode is oriented to true north and used for route verification?

options.text: VOR
MAP
PLAN
APP

explanation: A fixed orientation makes it possible to check the shape of the route as entered, independent of where the airplane is pointing.

question: Which navigation display mode presents raw ILS deviation information?

options.text: VOR
PLAN
MAP
APP

explanation: Displaying the raw signal allows the approach to be flown and monitored without reference to the computed route.

question: What do the data selection switches on the display control panel add to the navigation display?

options.text: Additional engine parameters
Optional overlays such as airports, waypoints, navigation aids and weather
The standby instrument indications
The autopilot mode annunciations

explanation: Each overlay is selected only when it is needed, since displaying everything at once makes the picture unreadable.

question: Why is the weather radar display range selection significant?

options.text: Because the radar cannot transmit beyond the selected range
Because the radar tilt is linked to the range selection
Because the range selection changes the radar frequency
Because the radar picture is drawn to the selected range and detail changes with it

explanation: Assessing weather requires looking at more than one range, since a short range picture can hide what lies beyond it.

question: What is the purpose of the standby flight instruments?

options.text: They provide attitude, airspeed and altitude independently of the main display system
They provide a backup for the flight management computer
They provide a second navigation display for the observer
They provide engine indications after a display failure

explanation: An independent path to the basic flying information is what allows flight to continue after a display system failure.

question: From what are the standby instruments normally powered?

options.text: The main AC transfer buses
The galley bus
The standby electrical system, which is backed by the battery
They require no electrical power at all

explanation: They must survive the same failures that remove the main displays, which is why they are on the protected supply.

question: What does an integrated standby flight display present?

options.text: Attitude, airspeed, altitude and approach guidance in one instrument
Navigation and engine data
Attitude only
Airspeed and altitude only

explanation: Combining the functions reduces the panel space required while keeping the information independent of the main system.

question: What is the role of the standby magnetic compass?

options.text: It is used only during ground compass swinging
It provides the primary heading source for the displays
It provides a heading reference independent of electrical power
It supplies heading data to the inertial reference system

explanation: Its independence from every airplane system is exactly what makes it valuable after a total electrical failure.

question: What do the air data inertial reference units provide?

options.text: Both air data and inertial position and attitude information
Inertial position only
Air data only
Navigation database information

explanation: Combining the two functions in one unit gives a single validated source of both the air mass and the inertial picture.

question: Which sensors supply the air data function?

options.text: The flight management computer database
Pitot probes, static ports, angle of attack vanes and the total air temperature probe
The radio altimeter and the ILS receiver
The inertial platform alone

explanation: Every air data output is derived from these physical inputs, which is why their heating and their condition matter so much.

question: What is required for an inertial reference alignment?

options.text: The airplane must be aligned with the runway heading
The airplane must remain stationary
The engines must be running
The flight management computer must contain an active route

explanation: The system is measuring the rotation of the earth to find north, and any airplane movement corrupts that measurement.

question: What affects the time required for an inertial alignment?

options.text: The number of units being aligned
The electrical source in use
The latitude at which the alignment is performed
The outside air temperature

explanation: The earth rotation component that the system measures changes with latitude. Verify the alignment times against your operator FCOM.

question: What is the attitude mode of the inertial reference system used for?

options.text: Providing attitude and heading after the navigation function has been lost
Providing a backup air data source
Transferring attitude information between the two units
Aligning the system in flight to restore full navigation

explanation: It recovers the most critical output, attitude, even though position and true heading cannot be recovered in flight.

question: What does the crew have to provide when using the attitude mode?

options.text: A manual heading input
A manual position update
An airspeed input from the standby instruments
A magnetic variation entry

explanation: Without a valid alignment the system has no heading reference of its own, so the crew supplies it from the standby compass.

question: Why can a full inertial alignment not be performed in flight?

options.text: Because the units cannot be cooled in flight
Because the alignment requires a position entry from the ground crew
Because the units are powered only on the ground
Because the system cannot separate airplane motion from the earth rotation it is measuring

explanation: The alignment depends on the platform being still, which is a condition that cannot exist in flight.

question: What is the purpose of the source select switches for air data and inertial data?

options.text: They select between the standby and main instruments
They select the navigation source for the flight director
They transfer the displays between the two display electronic units
They allow both flight displays to be fed from a single remaining source

explanation: Feeding both sides from one source keeps both pilots displaying valid data after a single unit fails.

question: Why is an annunciation displayed when both sides are fed from a single source?

options.text: Because the selected source is degraded
Because the standby instruments become the primary reference
Because the autopilot cannot be engaged in that configuration
Because the independence between the two pilot displays has been lost

explanation: Two displays showing the same data can no longer cross check each other, and the crew must know that the agreement is meaningless.

question: What is the purpose of the instrument comparison monitors?

options.text: They compare the selected and actual autopilot modes
They compare the two sides and flag a disagreement in airspeed, altitude, attitude or heading
They compare the displayed data with the standby instruments
They compare the flight director command with the actual flight path

explanation: An erroneous source is dangerous precisely because it looks normal, and the comparison is what exposes it.

question: What is the correct interpretation of an airspeed disagreement flag?

options.text: At least one of the two sources is wrong and neither can be assumed correct
The captain source is always the valid one
The disagreement is normal in turbulence and can be ignored
The standby instrument has failed

explanation: The flag says only that the two differ, so the resolution requires a third reference and a known pitch and thrust setting.

question: Why is a third airspeed reference so valuable in an unreliable airspeed situation?

options.text: Because it is the only source approved for instrument flight
Because it is the source used by the autopilot
Because it is more accurate than the primary sources
Because two disagreeing sources cannot be resolved without it

explanation: With three references the odd one out can usually be identified, which is not possible with only two.

question: How is invalid or missing data presented on the displays?

options.text: By the indication freezing at its last value
By the indication flashing in green
By a flag or by removal of the affected indication
By an amber outline around the whole display

explanation: Removing data that cannot be trusted is safer than displaying a value the crew might act on.

question: Why is a frozen indication more dangerous than a flagged one?

options.text: Because it cannot be cleared by the crew
Because it prevents the display from being transferred
Because it disables the comparison monitors
Because it continues to look valid while no longer reflecting reality

explanation: A flag prompts a response, whereas a plausible but static value invites the crew to keep trusting it.

question: What is the function of the barometric reference setting on the display control panel?

options.text: It selects between radio and barometric minimums
It sets the pressure datum used by the altitude display
It sets the cabin altitude warning threshold
It sets the minimum descent altitude

explanation: The altitude shown is only as correct as the datum entered, which is why the setting is cross checked between pilots.

question: Why are the barometric settings cross checked between the two pilots?

options.text: Because each side has its own setting and an error would not otherwise be detected
Because the settings are linked and must be changed together
Because only one setting feeds the altitude alerting system
Because the standby altimeter uses the captain setting

explanation: Independent settings provide the redundancy, and the cross check is what turns that redundancy into protection.

question: What does the vertical speed indication show?

options.text: The vertical path deviation from the computed profile
The rate of change of cabin altitude
The vertical speed selected on the mode control panel
The rate of change of altitude

explanation: It is the derivative of the altitude indication, and it responds faster than the altitude tape to a change in the flight path.

question: What is the value of the vertical path deviation indication during a descent?

options.text: It shows whether the airplane is above or below the computed vertical profile
It replaces the vertical speed indication in VNAV
It shows the vertical speed required to reach the selected altitude
It shows the glideslope deviation before capture

explanation: Managing the descent is a matter of energy, and knowing the displacement from the profile is what allows an early correction.

question: What are the pointers selectable on the navigation display used to show?

options.text: The autopilot commanded heading
The great circle track to the destination
The wind direction and speed
Bearing to selected VOR or ADF stations

explanation: Raw bearing information supports position awareness independently of the computed navigation solution.

question: What information does the display give about the wind?

options.text: Only the forecast wind from the flight plan
Direction and speed relative to the airplane track
Only the headwind or tailwind component
The wind at the destination airport

explanation: The wind is computed from the difference between the inertial and air data solutions, and it feeds both navigation and performance decisions.

question: Why does a loss of one inertial reference unit not remove the attitude display on both sides?

options.text: Because attitude is derived from the air data computers
Because the standby instrument feeds both primary displays
Because the flight control computers provide a backup attitude reference
Because each side is normally fed by its own unit, with switching available if one fails

explanation: The independence of the two sources is what makes a single failure recoverable through switching.

question: Why is the display system described as reconfigurable rather than redundant alone?

options.text: Because the standby instruments can replace any display
Because the display electronic units switch automatically without crew action
Because the crew can move the information to a working display when a unit fails
Because each display can show any format automatically

explanation: Reconfiguration means the number of failures that leave the crew without essential information is very small.
